transcript:
Meeting: Redpine x Redwood — POC scoping (representative load + perf baseline mapping)
Recorded: 2026-02-06 10:00am PT
Duration: 56 minutes
Attendees:
- Henry Cho (Redwood)
- Noah Patel (Redwood)
- Claire Dubois (Redwood)
- Priya Nair (Redpine)
- Evan Li (Redpine)
- Marta Gomez (Redpine)

Summary (auto-generated):
- Redpine shared 3 primary LLM workloads (streaming chat for support agents, non-streaming summarization, long-context document Q&A) and peak/baseline concurrency.
- Redwood mapped Redpine’s patterns to Redwood’s internal representative traffic shapes (short streaming, mixed prompt lengths, long-context streaming, bursty concurrency).
- Agreed on POC benchmark plan: run suite on Dedicated in us-east-1, measure TTFT/TPOT/E2E, include warm vs cold cache phases, and produce a short report + raw artifacts.

Topics (auto-generated):
- Traffic patterns: prompt length distribution, output length distribution, streaming usage
- Concurrency + burst behavior, time-of-day spikes, mixed tenants
- Success criteria and what “p99” means for streaming
- Benchmarking plan + environment pinning

Questions (auto-generated):
- How do we define TTFT for streaming (server vs client clock)?
- Can we emulate production cache hit rates without storing prompts?
- What hardware SKU is representative for Dedicated?

Action items (auto-generated):
- Redwood to send POC plan + runner config; Redpine to confirm regions and share token stats.


[00:00] Henry Cho: Cool, alright. Thanks everyone for making time. This is the POC scoping one, specifically to make sure we benchmark what you actually run, not like a toy “hello world” benchmark.

[00:12] Priya Nair: Sounds good.

[00:13] Evan Li: Yep.

[00:15] Marta Gomez: Hey, hi.

[00:17] Henry Cho: Quick intros—Henry, I’m on the product side but I own the customer-facing performance stuff. Noah is our runtime perf architect, Claire works on the representative workload suite design. So if we get into the weeds on distributions, that’s them.

[00:31] Noah Patel: Hey all.

[00:32] Claire Dubois: Hi.

[00:35] Henry Cho: Priya, want to give the 60-second overview of what you’re trying to prove in the POC?

[00:40] Priya Nair: Sure. So we have a support agent product, internal-ish, but it’s customer-facing indirectly. Latency is huge—agents complain. We also have an “analyst copilot” where they upload docs, ask questions, sometimes pretty long context. We’re evaluating Dedicated vs just using a managed API. We’ve been on… some Bedrock endpoints and we tried Together. We want a clear p95 and p99 story under load, not just single-request latency.

[01:10] Henry Cho: Great. And today we’ll capture (1) traffic shapes and (2) success metrics. Then we’ll propose an actual run matrix.

[01:19] Evan Li: Yup.

[01:21] Henry Cho: Evan, can you break down the routes? Like, what are the top 2–3 endpoints in your app, and what % of traffic.

[01:28] Evan Li: Yeah. Roughly three:
1) “SupportChat” route: streaming chat completions, multi-turn, but per request the prompt is usually not insane, like 300 to 1,200 tokens? Sometimes it spikes because we stuff in the ticket history.
2) “CaseSummary”: non-streaming summarization of a case. Prompt is bigger—maybe 2k to 6k tokens. Output is like 200 to 600 tokens.
3) “DocQA”: long context doc Q&A. That’s the scary one. Prompt can be 12k to 60k tokens depending on how much we cram. Output is usually short, like 100-300 tokens, but sometimes they ask for like a table and it becomes 800.

[02:16] Claire Dubois: When you say prompt tokens, is that including your system prompt and tool schema and everything? Or just user+context.

[02:23] Evan Li: That’s total. Well… it’s what we see from our tokenizer in the client, so it includes system. We use a fairly standard chat template.

[02:32] Noah Patel: And model-wise, are you targeting one model across all three? Or different model classes.

[02:37] Evan Li: We expect two. For SupportChat we want something fast; for DocQA we need long context. We’re open on exact model. We’ve been using like “70B-ish” for quality, but cost is high.

[02:52] Henry Cho: Totally. For POC we can pick one or two from our catalog that match those. The key is the load pattern.

[03:00] Marta Gomez: And concurrency. That’s the other piece.

[03:02] Henry Cho: Yes. Let’s do concurrency next. Marta, do you have numbers on baseline vs peak.

[03:07] Marta Gomez: Yeah. So… we have a weekday shape. Normal is like 20-40 concurrent active agent sessions. Peak can jump when shift changes, like 150-ish concurrent sessions. But “concurrent sessions” isn’t exactly concurrent requests. It’s more like how many people are typing.

[03:26] Noah Patel: Right, so we want request rate or simultaneous in-flight requests. For streaming, sessions can overlap a lot.

[03:34] Marta Gomez: Exactly. If I look at our gateway, SupportChat peak is maybe 60 requests per second for short bursts? But a lot are cancellations because the agent changes the prompt.

[03:47] Evan Li: Yeah, there’s a lot of stop-generation and retry. Like they hit backspace and re-send.

[03:53] Claire Dubois: That’s actually important; cancellations affect scheduling and tail latency. Do you know what fraction are canceled.

[03:59] Evan Li: Not precise. Maybe 10 to 20% of streaming generations are canceled before completion.

[04:08] Noah Patel: Great datapoint.

[04:10] Henry Cho: And for CaseSummary and DocQA, are those interactive or batch.

[04:15] Priya Nair: CaseSummary is triggered by the UI, but non-streaming is okay as long as it’s consistent. DocQA is interactive but the user is okay waiting a bit—except they rage if it’s 2 minutes.

[04:29] Henry Cho: So what’s “okay” in numbers. p95, p99.

[04:33] Priya Nair: For SupportChat, we care about time-to-first-token. If first token takes more than… 800ms p95, people complain. p99 ideally under 1.5 seconds. And then tokens per second should be stable, like 25+ tok/sec.

[04:52] Noah Patel: Got it. And are you measuring TTFT client-side.

[04:55] Marta Gomez: Yes, we measure from request send to first chunk received. But there’s some buffering weirdness depending on the SDK.

[05:03] Noah Patel: That matches what we usually recommend: client-perceived TTFT. We’ll also record server-side for debugging, but we’ll align to your method.

[05:11] Claire Dubois: For DocQA, what’s the p95/p99 target? It’s long prefill so TTFT will be larger.

[05:19] Evan Li: Honestly if it’s like 3-5 seconds TTFT for huge contexts that’s acceptable. But p99 can’t be like 30 seconds randomly.

[05:30] Priya Nair: And for end-to-end, for the whole answer, we prefer under 20 sec for the long one. But that’s flexible.

[05:39] Henry Cho: Great. So we have clear SLO-ish targets. Now, what we’ll do is map these to our internal “traffic shapes” so the POC is apples-to-apples with our baseline suite.

[05:52] Claire Dubois: I’ll translate what I heard into shapes.
- Shape A: “Short streaming chat, mixed prompt length” — prompt 300-1,200 tokens, output maybe 150-400 tokens, streaming on, with ~10-20% cancellations.
- Shape B: “Medium non-streaming summarize” — prompt 2k-6k, output 200-600.
- Shape C: “Long-context interactive” — prompt 12k-60k, output 100-300, streaming maybe on? you said interactive.

[06:21] Evan Li: For DocQA we do streaming today, yes.

[06:24] Claire Dubois: OK, streaming on for Shape C.

[06:27] Noah Patel: And the concurrency regime: you said 60 rps bursts for chat, plus session overlap. We can model that as a concurrency ramp with bursts and then steady state. For instance: ramp from 20 to 150 concurrent streaming requests over 2 minutes, hold, then drop. Does that resemble.

[06:47] Marta Gomez: Pretty close. But the burst is sharper, like within 20-30 seconds.

[06:52] Noah Patel: Perfect, we can do a steeper ramp.

[06:55] Henry Cho: One key thing: are you single-tenant or multi-tenant across products. Like do these routes compete for the same model capacity.

[07:03] Priya Nair: Yes, they compete. It’s one shared pool today.

[07:07] Noah Patel: That matters because mixing long-prefill with short chat can cause head-of-line blocking if the scheduler isn’t careful. We’ll explicitly test mixed-tenant mode.

[07:16] Evan Li: That’s actually what we see on Bedrock sometimes. Like chat gets slow when someone runs a big doc query.

[07:23] Henry Cho: Exactly. So we’ll run a “mixed workload” scenario: 70% Shape A, 20% Shape B, 10% Shape C, and we’ll also vary it to stress long-context.

[07:35] Claire Dubois: We generally define these mixes as a canonical “mixed tenants” traffic shape with configurable weights. We don’t need your prompts, we just need token distributions.

[07:44] Priya Nair: I want to double click the prompt thing. We can’t share real prompts. Even anonymized is hard.

[07:50] Henry Cho: Yep, understood. We do not need raw prompts. For representative load we do synthetic prompts and/or sanitized templates. What we need is: (a) token counts distribution, (b) streaming yes/no, (c) concurrency/time pattern, (d) stop/cancel rate, and optionally cache behavior.

[08:09] Marta Gomez: Cache behavior meaning what.

[08:12] Noah Patel: Prefix cache / KV cache hits. For example, do you have repeated system prompts, repeated tool schemas, repeated first turns. Many chat apps have like 30-60% prefix reuse.

[08:24] Evan Li: Yeah we have a static system prompt and tool schema. User content changes but the first ~400 tokens are stable.

[08:31] Claire Dubois: Great. That means we should include a warm-cache phase. We can do: warm-up run for 10 minutes to establish steady-state cache, then measure. And also a cold-start run.

[08:43] Priya Nair: Cold-start is important because we autoscale.

[08:47] Noah Patel: Right. In Dedicated, cold-start is a bit different (capacity is reserved), but you still get cold cache after deploys or node rotation. We can simulate by clearing caches between trials.

[08:59] Henry Cho: Let’s talk about geography and deployment mode. Are you expecting Dedicated in a specific region.

[09:05] Priya Nair: us-east-1 primarily. Maybe eu-west later, but POC can be US.

[09:11] Henry Cho: OK. And you’re evaluating Dedicated versus hosted shared API.

[09:16] Priya Nair: Yes. Hosted is easier but we worry about noisy neighbors and p99. Dedicated we want the SLA.

[09:25] Henry Cho: Makes sense.

[09:27] Evan Li: Also we need audit logs and encryption, but that’s a separate call.

[09:31] Henry Cho: Yep—we’ll keep this one performance. We can schedule security review separately.

[09:37] Noah Patel: Let me ask hardware: if you’re on Dedicated, are you OK with H100, or are you expecting A100 due to cost.

[09:45] Priya Nair: We want to understand both. Like cost/perf trade. But start with whichever is “best practice.”

[09:52] Henry Cho: We’ll start with H100 for peak performance and a second run on A100 if needed. For the POC we can keep it simple: one SKU in one region, then optional follow-up.

[10:05] Marta Gomez: We care about variance too. Like run-to-run jitter. On Together we saw p99 just jump around.

[10:13] Noah Patel: That’s part of why we’ve been building a variance budget and a reproducible harness. In the POC, we’ll do multiple trials, same environment pins. We’ll report mean and confidence interval, not just a single number.

[10:27] Claire Dubois: Concretely, we usually do: warmup, then 5 to 10 measured trials per shape, each trial 10 minutes steady-state. For p99 you need enough samples.

[10:39] Evan Li: That’s a lot of runs.

[10:41] Noah Patel: We can prioritize. For example:
- Shape A (SupportChat) is top priority: do 10 trials.
- Shape C (Long-context streaming) 5 trials.
- Mixed workload scenario 5 trials.
- Shape B maybe 3 trials if time.

[10:59] Henry Cho: And we can fit that into a few hours of runtime if we schedule it. Plus overnight if needed.

[11:05] Priya Nair: OK.

[11:07] Henry Cho: Let’s clarify what metrics we’ll deliver. We usually give:
- TTFT p50/p95/p99 (client-perceived)
- TPOT (time per output token) and tokens/sec
- End-to-end latency for non-streaming
- Throughput at fixed latency thresholds
- Error rates and throttles
- And some “explainability” metrics like queue wait and batch composition.

[11:31] Marta Gomez: Queue wait is like… time in the scheduler before prefill.

[11:35] Noah Patel: Exactly.

[11:37] Evan Li: Can we also get cost per 1k tokens estimate.

[11:41] Henry Cho: For Dedicated it’s more like effective $ per million tokens based on utilization, but yes we can compute unit economics from throughput.

[11:51] Priya Nair: I want to avoid a benchmark that looks great but is unrealistic. Like if you use single-turn prompts but we’re multi-turn.

[11:59] Claire Dubois: Yep. Multi-turn mostly affects prompt growth and cache reuse. We can simulate multi-turn by constructing prompts with a conversation history distribution. We can do a “turn count distribution” like 1–8 turns, with average 4.

[12:15] Evan Li: That’s accurate. Most sessions are like 3-6 turns.

[12:20] Claire Dubois: Great. And we can model the “ticket history” injection as a long chunk appended occasionally—like 10% of turns add +2k tokens.

[12:32] Evan Li: Yes, that’s basically it.

[12:35] Noah Patel: And we’ll include cancellations: randomly stop 15% of streaming responses at, say, 30% completion. That changes how the KV cache is used and how the scheduler recovers.

[12:50] Marta Gomez: Do you simulate client disconnect.

[12:52] Noah Patel: We can. The runner can close the stream and send cancel. We’ll tag those as canceled so they don’t pollute the latency stats incorrectly.

[13:04] Henry Cho: There’s a subtle point: how do you define p99 for streaming—TTFT p99 or full completion p99.

[13:11] Priya Nair: Both, but TTFT is what the user perceives. Completion matters less, but still.

[13:17] Noah Patel: Ok, so for streaming we’ll report TTFT distribution and TPOT distribution. Completion time is basically TTFT + TPOT*(output tokens) but with streaming it can be weird.

[13:29] Evan Li: For us, if TPOT slows down mid-stream, it feels bad.

[13:33] Noah Patel: We’ll also report “inter-token gap” p95/p99 (time between chunks). That captures stutters.

[13:41] Marta Gomez: Nice. We measure something similar.

[13:44] Henry Cho: Cool.

[13:46] Priya Nair: What do you need from us to set up the distributions.

[13:50] Claire Dubois: Ideally:
- For each route, approximate histogram of prompt tokens (p50/p90/p99), output tokens (p50/p90/p99)
- Streaming yes/no
- For chat, distribution of turn count
- Peak concurrency and burst ramp time
- Cancellation rate
- Any must-have parameters like max context.

[14:16] Evan Li: We can pull p50/p95/p99 easily from logs but we have to be careful with privacy. Tokens counts are fine.

[14:23] Priya Nair: Yeah token counts are ok.

[14:25] Marta Gomez: We can also provide request rate graphs.

[14:28] Noah Patel: Perfect.

[14:30] Henry Cho: Great. Now, let’s talk about the actual POC environment. We can run this in our Dedicated environment, pinned driver/CUDA versions. We’ll share the run metadata and config so it’s reproducible.

[14:45] Evan Li: Is that like a report plus raw json.

[14:48] Henry Cho: Exactly. Raw artifacts plus a summary doc.

[14:52] Marta Gomez: Can we run from our VPC to get real network path.

[14:56] Noah Patel: We can do two modes:
1) Runner inside the same region (close to servers) to reduce network noise.
2) Runner from your environment to measure true client-perceived.
We usually do (1) for stable comparisons, then a smaller (2) for realistic E2E.

[15:17] Priya Nair: We care about (2), but I get the point about noise.

[15:21] Henry Cho: We can do both. We’ll be clear what each number means.

[15:26] Evan Li: On Together, we saw p99 TTFT jump because of network jitter, so it’s hard.

[15:33] Noah Patel: Yep.

[15:35] Claire Dubois: Another question: tool calling. Do you do function/tool calls that cause multiple generations.

[15:41] Evan Li: Yes, in SupportChat we sometimes call a ticket lookup tool. That adds like a second request. But it’s not constant.

[15:49] Henry Cho: For this POC, we can benchmark the base model generation and then if you want we can simulate tool-calling as a multi-step workflow. But step one is “single generation request performance.”

[16:03] Priya Nair: Agreed.

[16:05] Marta Gomez: Also we have bursts where a batch job runs summaries on like 2,000 cases.

[16:11] Evan Li: Yeah that’s the CaseSummary route. It’s batch but time sensitive.

[16:16] Noah Patel: That’s an important separate shape: non-streaming, high throughput, high batching pressure. We can add a “batch summarization” traffic shape: high QPS, shorter outputs, concurrency like 200-500.

[16:30] Priya Nair: That might compete with chat though.

[16:32] Noah Patel: Exactly, we can test it both isolated and mixed.

[16:36] Henry Cho: OK, I’m going to sanity check time. We have about 40 minutes left. Let’s lock down the benchmark plan. Noah, can you propose a matrix.

[16:45] Noah Patel: Sure. Proposed POC plan (v1):
Environment:
- Dedicated cluster, us-east-1
- Hardware: H100 (80GB) as primary; optional A100 follow-up
- Runtime build pinned (we’ll stamp commit SHA), fixed driver/CUDA

Workloads:
1) Shape A: SupportChat streaming
   - Prompt tokens: sample from distribution (p50 600, p95 1,200, p99 2,500) — you’ll confirm numbers
   - Output tokens: p50 250, p95 450
   - Turn count distribution: 1–8
   - Cancellation: 15%
   - Concurrency: ramp 30 -> 180 in 30 seconds, hold 10 min, then drop
   - Metrics: TTFT, inter-token gap, TPOT, errors

2) Shape C: DocQA long-context streaming
   - Prompt: p50 18k, p95 45k, p99 60k (confirm)
   - Output: p50 180, p95 400
   - Concurrency: 5 -> 40, hold
   - Include warm-cache and cold-cache runs

3) Mixed scenario
   - 70% A, 20% B (CaseSummary), 10% C
   - Concurrency scaled to match peak

4) Optional: Batch summaries
   - Non-streaming, high QPS

Run structure:
- Warmup 5 minutes
- 5–10 measured trials per workload
- Rerun any trial with environment drift signals (GPU SKU mismatch etc.)

Deliverables:
- Summary report (tables + graphs)
- Raw JSON artifacts (per-trial)
- Runner config and seed so it’s reproducible

[18:35] Priya Nair: That’s good. On DocQA concurrency, 40 might be high, but okay to test.

[18:41] Evan Li: Prompt p50 18k sounds right, p95 maybe 35k more than 45k. But we’ll confirm.

[18:48] Claire Dubois: Great, we’ll tune it.

[18:50] Marta Gomez: Can you explain the cache part. For DocQA, cache hits are low because the docs change.

[18:56] Noah Patel: Right, but for chat the prefix is stable. So we’ll do warm-cache primarily for chat. For DocQA, we might just do cold-cache. Or we do a small warm-cache with repeated system prefix, but the long context part will still be unique.

[19:12] Claire Dubois: We can parameterize “prefix reuse ratio.” For chat maybe 0.6; for docQA maybe 0.1.

[19:20] Priya Nair: Sounds right.

[19:23] Henry Cho: You mentioned p99 requirements. I want to make sure we agree what’s a pass. For SupportChat you said TTFT p95 < 800ms, p99 < 1.5s. Is that at peak concurrency.

[19:36] Priya Nair: Yes, at peak.

[19:38] Evan Li: But we can accept slightly worse p99 if it’s extremely rare. Like 99.9 matters too but we don’t have data.

[19:46] Noah Patel: We can measure p99 and approximate p99.9 if we have enough samples. But p99.9 takes a lot of volume.

[19:54] Henry Cho: For POC we’ll focus on p99 and we’ll look at the tail shape.

[20:00] Marta Gomez: Also, what about retries. If you load shed, we want graceful error codes.

[20:07] Noah Patel: Good point. Under overload, we can test load-shedding policy. We’ll report error rates and specific backpressure events. In Dedicated we can set a “no shed” mode to see raw behavior, but production should shed rather than blow up latency.

[20:24] Priya Nair: We prefer a fast error over a 30 second hang.

[20:28] Henry Cho: Same.

[20:30] Evan Li: The other question: how does your benchmark runner compare to our real client. We use a Node client with SSE streaming.

[20:38] Noah Patel: Our runner can do SSE and websockets; also we can run a simple Node harness to match exactly. For TTFT definition, we’ll instrument both ends.

[20:49] Marta Gomez: Our TTFT includes TLS handshake sometimes.

[20:52] Noah Patel: For fair comparison, we should separate connection setup from request timing. We can reuse keep-alives. But we can also report both.

[21:02] Priya Nair: Please do. We’ll be behind a proxy.

[21:06] Henry Cho: OK.

[21:08] Claire Dubois: One more detail: you mentioned mixed tenants. Do you have separate “priority” classes. Like chat should preempt batch summaries.

[21:17] Priya Nair: Ideally yes. Today we don’t have a good story.

[21:21] Noah Patel: We can implement priority routing in Dedicated. For POC we can run both “fair share” and “priority chat” to show tail improvements.

[21:34] Evan Li: That would be compelling.

[21:36] Henry Cho: It also ties into your p99 requirement.

[21:39] Marta Gomez: How do you ensure the results aren’t just good because you turned off batching or something.

[21:45] Noah Patel: We’ll keep a documented batching policy. For each run, we record batch size distribution, prefill/decode utilization, queue depth. If a run improves, we can show why.

[21:59] Claire Dubois: And the harness will label the traffic shape and the runtime configuration in the artifact so it’s auditable.

[22:07] Priya Nair: Ok.

[22:09] Henry Cho: Let’s talk timeline. We’re Feb 6. When do you want results.

[22:14] Priya Nair: We want to make a decision by end of month. Ideally first results next week.

[22:21] Henry Cho: We can do that. If we can provision Dedicated early next week, we can run mid-week and deliver by Friday.

[22:29] Evan Li: That works.

[22:31] Marta Gomez: We need to do vendor review too. But yes.

[22:35] Henry Cho: Great.

[22:36] (crosstalk)

[22:38] Noah Patel: Quick note: long-context runs can be time-consuming. But we’ll schedule them first so we don’t slip.

[22:46] Claire Dubois: Also: we need to pick the model(s). For chat, do you want “best latency” or “best quality.”

[22:53] Evan Li: In POC, pick one that’s comparable to what we use today. Like a 70B class. But also maybe a smaller one if it’s dramatically faster.

[23:04] Henry Cho: OK, we’ll do two models for SupportChat: one “quality” and one “fast.” For DocQA we’ll use the long-context capable one.

[23:14] Priya Nair: That’s fine.

[23:16] Marta Gomez: How do we ensure the model is the same across providers. Like comparing to OpenAI or Bedrock is not same.

[23:23] Henry Cho: It won’t be identical. The POC is to see if Redwood meets your latency SLOs and throughput at acceptable cost. For apples-to-apples across vendors, we can do a small comparative run later, but we usually avoid “benchmark wars” because models differ.

[23:38] Priya Nair: Understood.

[23:40] Evan Li: We still need to show leadership that it’s competitive.

[23:43] Henry Cho: Totally. We can include a “reference run” using your existing endpoint, if you can run the same synthetic workload from your side and share results. But that’s optional.

[23:56] Marta Gomez: We can do that. We already have some load test infra.

[24:00] Noah Patel: Great. If you do, be careful with clock sync and network. But it’s useful.

[24:06] Claire Dubois: For synthetic prompts, do you care about content. Like does it need to be domain-specific.

[24:12] Evan Li: Not really. As long as tokenization and structure is similar (tables, JSON sometimes).

[24:19] Claire Dubois: We can include some “structured output” prompts (like JSON schema) because that can change decode behavior.

[24:27] Evan Li: Yes, we do that.

[24:29] Henry Cho: Good catch.

[24:31] Priya Nair: Another nuance: we have a lot of short “classification-ish” prompts too, but they’re small volume.

[24:38] Noah Patel: We can ignore for now. If it becomes relevant we add later.

[24:44] Henry Cho: Ok.

[24:46] Marta Gomez: Can you talk about error cases: timeouts, retries.

[24:50] Noah Patel: Sure. In the runner, we’ll set explicit client timeout and we’ll track:
- timeouts
- server 5xx
- 429/backpressure
- cancellation
We’ll also track any “stall” where streaming pauses > X seconds.

[25:10] Marta Gomez: Nice.

[25:12] Priya Nair: One more question: can you run the workload suite with mixed prompt lengths in the same batch. That’s realistic.

[25:20] Noah Patel: Yes, and it’s exactly one of our shapes. Mixed prompt lengths increases fragmentation and can hurt batching. We’ll include it.

[25:28] Claire Dubois: The generator samples prompt lengths from a mixture distribution, not a fixed length. So it will be realistic.

[25:35] Evan Li: Good.

[25:37] Henry Cho: Cool. Let’s do a quick recap of what we need from you by early next week.

[25:43] Henry Cho: Evan: token distributions for the 3 routes, plus turn counts. Marta: concurrency ramp and peak QPS estimate plus cancellation fraction. Priya: confirm success thresholds and region.

[25:55] Priya Nair: Yes.

[25:56] Evan Li: Yes.

[25:58] Marta Gomez: Yep.

[26:00] Henry Cho: And from us: we send the one-pager POC plan, plus a sample runner config, plus access once Dedicated is provisioned.

[26:10] Noah Patel: And we’ll propose the exact trial counts and how we compute variance.

[26:14] Claire Dubois: Also we’ll include a section “what is representative vs synthetic” so it passes your internal review.

[26:20] Priya Nair: That helps.

[26:22] (pause)

[26:24] Evan Li: Can I ask about streaming TTFT definition. On some providers, first token is buffered until they have like 5 tokens.

[26:31] Noah Patel: Yes, chunking. We can control chunking in our API. For the benchmark, we’ll configure chunk size = 1 token equivalent, or “flush on token.” But if your client buffers, you’ll still see chunking. That’s why we want a small Node harness too.

[26:49] Marta Gomez: Our proxy buffers too.

[26:52] Noah Patel: Then we’ll measure both server-side and client-side so you can separate buffering effects.

[27:00] Henry Cho: Perfect.

[27:02] Priya Nair: Great.

[27:05] Henry Cho: Anything else you want to cover.

[27:08] Evan Li: Not right now.

[27:10] Marta Gomez: No.

[27:12] Priya Nair: I think that’s it.
